recommendations: Run g01 to g06 in outline order after the trigonometry strand, then s01 to s11. Probability needs nothing from the other strands except fractions and listing, so s01 to s11 can be designed in parallel with any strand.

Joins: g01 opens on a parent graph from w15 (its join from t16 is fixed when t16 is designed); g02 to g06 each open on the previous final frame; s01 follows g06 in the playlist but starts a new topic, so its opening does not depend on g06.
Shared point cid4fd3807: g04 owns the function rule after a described sequence and describing the transformations; g05 owns domain, range, intercepts, asymptotes and discontinuities of the result.

Year 12 entry knowledge delivered here: g01 to g04 (translations, reflections, dilations and their order, read as y = k f(a(x + b)) + c with the inside factored first; Year 12 t01, d02, d13); s04 (sample spaces, P(A) = |A|/|S|), s05 (complement rule, Year 12 s04), s06 (the two-dice array, Year 12 s02), s09 (random variables, Year 12 s01), s10 (relative frequency, Year 12 s01) and s11 (histograms, Year 12 s01 and s04).

Possible splits if drafts run long: g05 (polynomials and |x| apart from hyperbolas, exponentials and logs), s07 (counting form and Venn restriction apart from two-way tables and trees), s08 (the two proofs apart from practical problems). Possible merge: s02 with s03.

Thirteen site findings are logged as S11-G01 to S11-G06 and S11-P01 to S11-P07 in section 8 of site-corrections-maths-a11.md (three of them minor); notation differences and content gaps are listed there too.
covers: math-a11-g01 to math-a11-g06 (Graph transformations) and math-a11-s01 to math-a11-s11 (Probability and data)

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: Which way does replacing x by x - a move a graph?

syllabusActions.text: Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x - a in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal translation of a graph by a, that replacing y by y - b corresponds to a vertical translation by b, and recognise that the sign of a and b determines the direction of the translation
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x-a in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal translation of a graph by a, that replacing y by y-b corresponds to a vertical translation by b, and recognise that the sign of a and b determines the direction of the translation

entryKnowledge.text: Vertex form y = a(x - h)^2 + k with vertex (h, k).
y = k/x with asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0.
Graphs of y = |x| and y = |ax + b| and their vertex.
Graphs of y = a^x with asymptote y = 0.
Domain and range in interval notation.

entries.startBoundary: A parent graph students already know, y = x^2 with its vertex at the origin (w15), and the question "does replacing x by x - 3 move it left or right?". The join from t16 is fixed when t16 is designed; g01 needs nothing from trigonometry.
entries.stopBoundary: Establish with a graphing application that replacing x by x - a in the equation of a graph is a horizontal translation by a and replacing y by y - b is a vertical translation by b, the sign of a and b giving the direction; apply it to y = x^2, |x|, 1/x and a^x (vertex, asymptotes and key points move with the graph; domain and range follow). Reflections are g02, dilations g03, sequences g04.
entries.recommendation: Keep the focused boundary and the site's exact worked-example numbers. Partial or missing site coverage needs original teaching. Old module labels are not the route. Claude chooses final splits and length. Teach the syllabus "replace y by y - b" form beside y = f(x) + b: both translations then share one rule (a minus sign moves the graph the positive way). Log S11-G01 before reusing site card 06.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do -x and -y reflect a graph?

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by -x in the equation of a graph corresponds to the reflection of the graph in the y-axis, and that replacing y by -y  corresponds to a reflection in the x-axis

Even and odd functions: unchanged by reflection in the y-axis or by a half-turn.
y = k a^(-x) as the reflection of y = k a^x.

entries.startBoundary: g01's final frame (a point and its translated image); now replace x by -x instead.
entries.stopBoundary: Establish with a graphing application that replacing x by -x reflects a graph in the y-axis and replacing y by -y reflects it in the x-axis; find images of points ((x, y) to (-x, y) and (x, -y)) and the equation of a reflected graph (every x replaced, in brackets); both together give (x, y) to (-x, -y). Even and odd tests stay in w26 (referenced, not re-taught).

syllabusActions.text: Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x/k in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal dilation of a graph by a factor of k, that replacing y by y/l corresponds to a vertical dilation by a factor of l, and determine the effects on the graph when the magnitude of the dilation factor lies between 0 and 1

syllabusActions.text: Establish, using graphing applications, replacing x by x/k and replacing y by y/k in the equation of a graph corresponds to a dilation by a factor of k, that is, an enlargement of the graph when k > 1 and a reduction of the graph when 0 < k < 1
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Establish, using graphing applications, replacing x by xk and replacing y by yk in the equation of a graph corresponds to a dilation by a factor of k, that is, an enlargement of the graph when k>1 and a reduction of the graph when 0<k<1

Images of points under a reflection.

y = ax^2 is narrower or wider than y = x^2.

entries.startBoundary: g02's final frame; a graph and the y-axis held fixed while every point moves away from it.
entries.stopBoundary: Describe a horizontal dilation as a stretch from the y-axis and a vertical dilation as a stretch from the x-axis; establish with a graphing application that replacing x by x/k is a horizontal dilation by factor k and replacing y by y/l a vertical dilation by factor l, including factors between 0 and 1 (compressions) and y = f(bx) as factor 1/b; establish that replacing x by x/k and y by y/k together is a dilation by factor k, an enlargement for k > 1 and a reduction for 0 < k < 1 (the unit circle becomes the circle of radius k). syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Recognise that the order in which individual transformations are applied to functions is important

syllabusActions.text: Apply reflections, translations and dilations to functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course, excluding trigonometric functions, determine the function rule and the graph of the transformed function, the domain and range of the transformed graph, any intercepts, asymptotes and discontinuities where appropriate, and describe which transformations have been applied

entryKnowledge.text: Translations by replacing x by x - a and y by y - b.
Reflections by replacing x by -x and y by -y.
Dilations by replacing x by x/k and y by y/l.

entries.startBoundary: Two copies of y = x^2 given the same two moves in opposite orders, ending at different vertices.
entries.stopBoundary: Recognise that the order of transformations matters (a translation and a dilation along the same axis do not commute; moves along different axes do); write the function rule after a described sequence of reflections, dilations and translations (not trigonometric functions), and describe the sequence from a rule by factoring the inside first (dilate, then translate). This video owns the "determine the function rule" and "describe which transformations have been applied" parts of cid4fd3807; domain, range, intercepts, asymptotes and discontinuities are g05.

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Identify an event A as a subset A of the sample space S

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Define the probability of each outcome to be 1S when all the outcomes are equally likely and the probability of the event A to be P A = A S

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: When are two events independent, and how do we prove it?

syllabusActions.text: Define two events to be independent if the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability that the other event occurs
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Define two events to be independent if the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability that the other event occurs

syllabusActions.text: Explain that two events A and B are independent means P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B), and show algebraically that if one of these formulas is true, then the other is also true

syllabusActions.text: Use the formula P(A|B) = (P(A ∩ B))/(P(B)), and the test P(A|B) = P(A) for independence to prove that if two events are independent, then P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), and to prove conversely that if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), then A and B are independent
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Use the formula PA|B=P(A∩B)P(B), and the test PAB=PA for independence to prove that if two events are independent, then PA∩B=PA×P(B), and to prove conversely that if PA∩B=PA×P(B), then A and B are independent
syllabusActions.siteGap: The product rule for independent events is stated and used. The proof in both directions from the conditional formula is not worked.

entries.stopBoundary: Define independent events (the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other); explain that independence means P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B) and show algebraically that one implies the other; prove that independence gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B) and the converse; solve practical problems; contrast with mutually exclusive events. Random variables are s09.

entries.stopBoundary: Define a random variable as a variable whose value is the outcome of a random experiment (X for the variable, x for a value, P(X = x)); compare discrete random variables (values that can be listed, usually counted, possibly infinitely many) with continuous ones (any value in an interval, usually measured), with practical examples of each.
